headlines.full_text: France is divided over who to blame for and what to learn from weekend riots In France and beyond there is widespread disagreement over what led to some of the worst unrest seen in French cities in modern history. "This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us'. That's not France!" Elisabeth was speaking to me in front of a row of smashed shop windows, shattered glass still littering the tree-lined Parisian street. Its walls were daubed with red-lettered graffiti insulting French police and signed with the date of the riots, 17 October. I'd stopped her and her friend to ask what they thought of what happened on Saturday. Elisabeth was so upset that, when she spoke, she seemed close to tears. "My friend thinks this is civil war in France but I don't. Saturday is about something else entirely." But what did happen exactly? Who was behind the riots? While much of the looting seemed opportunistic, the violence looked pre-planned. Why orchestrate it now, after weeks of student protests? And who most stands to gain from the destruction this weekend? Elisabeth wasn't entirely sure. Different theories are doing the rounds - in and outside France. Black and white answers may be appealing, but the truth is there are many factors at play. The president of the National Assembly, Yaël Braun-Pivet, has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised. French intelligence had briefed government circles earlier this month that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in the student protests. A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media report. The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday. The 34-year-old suspect is known to police for acts of violence against public officials and is on a French national security watchlist, FranceInfo and BFM TV report. Marseille mayor Benoît Payan said on X that the prefect had decided to introduce the curfew "starting this evening and for days to come", with French media reporting it would be in place overnight from Tuesday to Friday. Payan said the measures apply to minors and will only be in commercial areas of the city, which were particularly affected by looting which took place last weekend. Paris's police commissioner has also ordered the extension of an overnight curfew in the capital. The Préfecture de Police said the measure would continue "for as long as it proves necessary". A curfew for parts of central Lyon was renewed on Tuesday, while overnight curfews for Nice and Lille are ongoing, and a week-long, overnight curfew for Bordeaux came into force on Tuesday night. headlines.full_text: Seventh day of violent clashes between Albanian protesters and police Almost 300 people have been injured, more than half of them police, as violent anti-government demonstrations show no sign of easing. Protesters in Albania have fought with riot police on the seventh consecutive day of violent clashes. The protesters, many of them high school and university students, are trying to oust embattled Prime Minister Edi Rama. Official figures said 295 people have been injured, 186 of whom are police officers, before Monday's violence. "The moment the state negotiates with this," Rama told grim-faced police chiefs, brandishing a rock hurled at police on Sunday, "the state has fallen". A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked during the protests, which are being driven by demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and calls for Rama's resignation. The protesters included "young men and women who have been radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US", Rama said. "Albania has become one of the targets of a well co-ordinated attack." In brilliant October sunshine in Rinia Park, also known as Youth Park, I watched people prising loose cobble stones - like that brandished by the prime minister - as ammunition for later battles with police. They did not have long to wait. A convoy of police vehicles advanced down a broad boulevard, led by an armoured truck firing water cannon and tear gas canisters among the fleeing protesters. Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend. "The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said. Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people. More than 2,000 businesses were directly impacted by the weekend's violence, according to the head of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI). Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that the riots led to hundreds of millions of euros worth of damage. PETERSBURG, October 20. /TASS/. Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin has arrived in St. Petersburg for the 31st meeting of the heads of government of Russia and China. According to the Russian cabinet’s press service, Mishustin will hold talks with Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Wednesday. The parties will discuss pressing issues related to Russia-China relations of comprehensive partnership and strategic cooperation. Special attention will be paid to strengthening trade, economic, cultural and humanitarian cooperation and promoting joint projects in energy, industry agriculture, education and other fields. A joint communique and a number of bilateral documents will be adopted. Mishustin arrived in St. Petersburg from Tajikistan, where he took part in a meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Council of Heads of Government. In the Tajik capital, Dushanbe, he also held a meeting with Iranian First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref.
headlines.llm_reasoning: The piece simply reports the meeting details without bias or emotive language.

headlines.full_text: Current challenges play into Russian diplomats’ hands, mobilize them — Lavrov The top Russian diplomat added that the Russian Foreign Ministry and the entire foreign policy, determined by the president, face very difficult tasks MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov believes that the Chinese wish "God forbid you to live in interesting times" is not suitable for Russian diplomats, because the current challenges play into their hands and mobilize them. Lavrov told the university graduates who were hired for the first time into the diplomatic service that they joined the Foreign Ministry "at an interesting time. As the Chinese say, 'God forbid you to live in interesting times.' But we are not Chinese. Challenges are a boon to us, and we are always mobilized by the tasks that are becoming increasingly difficult." "At the current stage, the Russian Foreign Ministry, and the entire foreign policy determined by the president of the Russian Federation, face very difficult tasks. These are not easy times. You will have to immerse yourself in multi·layered, multifactorial, and ultra·fast processes right away, without any warming up. "If you are here, it means that you are determined, talented, and ambitious people. That’s good. You’re probably doing well in both languages and science. Now all this knowledge needs to be put into practice." He promised that the new generation of diplomats would be supported by "both veterans and the Council of young diplomats."

headlines.full_text: US church on front line of battle against drug known as 'tranq' Synthetic opioids like fentanyl are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape. America has been fighting the War on Drugs for decades, but the drug cartels, the suppliers and the dealers appear to be always one step ahead of the authorities. President Trump has declared the cartels, "terrorists" and labelled fentanyl, the powerful synthetic opioid, a "weapon of mass destruction". But the drug supply is changing, with other deadly synthetics being added to the mix, including strong animal tranquillisers, known on the streets as "tranq". While overdose deaths are falling, the potency of the new drugs has recovery workers worried. For some the answer might lie in reducing demand, giving users support and helping them end their addiction. BBC international correspondent Quentin Sommerville and camera journalist Darren Conway travelled to Columbus, Ohio to find out more. Read more on this story:A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis.

Under the new system, clocks will be allowed to drift from the Earth's actual rotation by up to an hour before anyone has to step in. This means no more leap seconds – for centuries. /VCG Leap seconds have been added to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) to keep it aligned with Earth's irregular rotation. But these adjustments can disrupt digital systems that rely on continuous, precise timekeeping. Since the practice began, 27 leap seconds have been inserted. In 2012, a leap second reportedly caused outages across more than 2,000 networks worldwide. In 2015, the US Intercontinental Exchange halted trading for more than 60 minutes. The risk of a negative leap second – removing a second rather than adding one – has also raised concerns, as computer systems have never had to implement one on a global scale. The reform comes after the 28th General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM), held in Versailles, France, adopted a resolution this month to introduce continuous UTC from May 20, 2027.
